The bill would update Australia's air cargo security rules to match international standards.
It would create a new type of industry participant, the known consignor, and give the government power to make regulations for approving them.
The changes are meant to keep Australian air freight competitive and avoid trade disruptions as global standards evolve.
Create two new categories of aviation industry participant: known consignor and regulated agent.
Define when cargo is cleared for transport on an aircraft.
Allow regulations to set up a scheme for approving known consignors.
Clarify that examining cargo may include opening or unpacking it.
Expand what the Secretary can cover in a notice.
Businesses that handle or arrange air cargo transport.

The Aviation Transport Security Amendment (Cargo) Bill 2015 was moved to amend the Aviation Transport Security Act 2004 to meet US requirements for 100% piece-level examination of air cargo on passenger flights, protecting $4.8 billion in Australian airfreight exports to the US. The government negotiated a two-year timeframe to implement changes, including a known consignor scheme and off-airport screening.

The speaker argued that the Aviation Transport Security Amendment (Cargo) Bill is necessary to balance aviation safety with economic efficiency, and that Labor supports it as a non-partisan measure. The bill creates a "known consignor" category to shift cargo screening responsibility to shippers, responding to US requirements that Australia meet item-by-item inspection standards for air cargo entering the United States.

The Aviation Transport Security Amendment (Cargo) Bill 2015 mandates 100% piece-level screening of air cargo on US-bound passenger flights and establishes a known consignor scheme, with Australia’s cargo security program recognised by the US until July 2017 to avoid disruption to $4.8 billion in annual air freight exports.

The Aviation Transport Security Amendment (Cargo) Bill 2015 requires 100% X-ray scanning of all air freight parcels destined for the United States, implemented through off-airport cargo examination by approved freight forwarders or a known consigner scheme. The measure, necessitated by US security requirements, supports $4.8 billion in Australian air exports to the US and is expected to provide a competitive advantage for exporters, including Tasmanian producers like Tasmanian Quality Meats.
The speaker supported the Aviation Transport Security Amendment (Cargo) Bill 2015 and praised the member for Lyons.

The Aviation Transport Security Amendment (Cargo) Bill 2015 establishes a known consignor program, streamlines air cargo clearance, and enhances cargo examinations to meet US Transportation Security Administration requirements, maintaining Australia's $4.8 billion annual airfreight export market to the USA. The speaker supported the bill, noting it balances necessary security upgrades—including potential 100% piece-level screening for US-bound cargo—against minimal regulatory burden, with a two-year industry adjustment period negotiated after US re-evaluation in December 2014.

The Aviation Transport Security Amendment (Cargo) Bill 2015 requires 100% screening of all cargo on passenger aircraft to meet US security standards, with a transition agreement extending to July 2017 to protect $4.8 billion in air freight exports. The bill establishes a known consignor scheme and allows exporters to choose screening methods to minimise costs and red tape.

The Aviation Transport Security Amendment (Cargo) Bill 2015 establishes a known consignor and regulated agent scheme to align Australia’s air cargo security with US and international standards, addressing a US finding that current arrangements fell short. Australia’s airfreight exports to the US are worth $4.8 billion, and the bill provides a two-year transition period to implement piece-level screening of all cargo on passenger aircraft.

The Aviation Transport Security Amendment (Cargo) Bill 2015 was introduced to align Australian air cargo security with US requirements, including 100% piece-level examination of cargo on passenger flights, via a known consignor scheme and off-airport screening, to protect $4.8 billion in airfreight exports to the United States.
